2.2 The first main result


By Proposition 2.2, the main conditions on \mathscr{L} to supply the induced evolution \dot{z}_{t}=\mathcal{A}(z_{t}) with a gradient structure are that the covector field \mathcal{V}(z) equals D_{s}\mathscr{L}(z,0), and that this covector field satisfies the integrability condition D_{s}\mathscr{L}(z,0)=D\mathcal{S}(z) for some \mathcal{S}. This leads to the following abstract result:


Theorem 2.3.

For any given L-function \mathscr{L} there holds:

(i) 

If the covector field D_{s}\mathscr{L}(z,0)=D\mathcal{S}_{\mathscr{L}}(z) for some \mathcal{S}_{\mathscr{L}}:\mathcal{Z}\to\mathbb{R}, and \Psi_{\mathscr{L}},\Psi^{*}_{\mathscr{L}} are constructed according to Lemma 2.3 with \mathcal{V}=D\mathcal{S}_{\mathscr{L}}, then (\mathcal{Z},\Psi_{\mathscr{L}},\mathcal{S}_{\mathscr{L}}) is a generalized gradient system that induces the evolution \dot{z}_{t}=\mathcal{A}_{\mathscr{L}}(z_{t}) and satisfies (2.2).

(ii) 

Moreover, any generalized gradient system (\mathcal{Z},\Psi,\mathcal{S}) inducing the evolution \dot{z}_{t}=\mathcal{A}_{\mathscr{L}}(z_{t}) and satisfying (2.2) equals (\mathcal{Z},\Psi_{\mathscr{L}},\mathcal{S}_{\mathscr{L}}), up to adding a constant to \mathcal{S}.

(iii) 

In addition, \Psi_{\mathscr{L}} is symmetric if and only if \mathscr{L} satisfies the time-symmetry condition (• ‣ ii).





Proof.

The theorem is a direct consequence of Lemma 2.3 and Proposition 2.2, using the covector field \mathcal{V}_{\mathscr{L}}=D\mathcal{S}_{\mathscr{L}}.
∎



We return to the interpretation of this theorem in the discussion in Section 5.


Remark 2.4. 
As discussed in the introduction of this section, we have assumed that \mathscr{L}(z,\cdot) is differentiable in 0. Many of these results generalize to the case where \mathscr{L}(z,\cdot) is convex, lower semicontinuous, and may attain the value +\infty. Then the subdifferential \partial_{s}\mathscr{L}(z,0):=\{\xi\in T^{*}_{z}\mathcal{Z}:\forall s\in T_{z}\mathcal{Z}\quad\mathscr{L}(z,s)\geq\mathscr{L}(z,0)+\langle\xi,s\rangle\} is well-defined, and for instance the condition D_{s}\mathscr{L}(z,0)=D\mathcal{S}(z) can be generalized to finding an \mathcal{S}_{\mathscr{L}} such that D\mathcal{S}_{\mathscr{L}}(z)\in\partial_{s}\mathscr{L}(z,0). In some cases \partial_{s}\mathscr{L}(z,0) may be empty. This happens for example if \mathscr{L} corresponds to the large-deviation rate functional of the empirical process on a finite state space \{1,\ldots,J\}, where the underlying Markov processes are reducible and the tangent space includes tangents of the form \mathds{1}_{\omega_{1}}-\mathds{1}_{\omega_{2}} for \omega_{1} and \omega_{2} from different irreducible components of \{1,\ldots,J\}.

∎

3.2 The second main result


From Section 2 we know that two conditions on L-functions play a crucial role in constructing a corresponding generalized gradient flow: the integrability condition (1.11) and the time-symmetry condition (• ‣ ii). We will now see that these two conditions are strongly related to the detailed balance condition of each X_{i}(t) (and hence of the empirical process \rho^{(n)}). We recall the definition here:


Definition 3.2.

A Markov process with generator \mathcal{Q} satisfies detailed balance with respect to a locally finite measure \pi if for all \psi,\phi\in\Dom\mathcal{Q} such that \mathcal{Q}(\phi\pi),\mathcal{Q}(\psi\pi)\in L^{1}(\pi),




\int_{\Omega}\!\phi(x)(\mathcal{Q}\psi)(x)\,\pi(dx)=\int_{\Omega}\!\psi(x)(\mathcal{Q}\phi)(x)\,\pi(dx).

(3.4)




Naturally, this definition immediately implies that \pi is invariant under \mathcal{Q}, i.e.




\int_{\Omega}\!(\mathcal{Q}\psi)\,d\pi=0\qquad\text{for all }\psi\in\Dom\mathcal{Q}\/\text{ such that }\mathcal{Q}\psi\in L^{1}(\pi).




With an invariant measure \pi at hand, one can construct the
relative entropy




\mathcal{E}_{\pi}(\rho):=\int_{\Omega}\!\log\frac{d\rho}{d\pi}(x)\,\rho(dx).

(3.5)

To avoid technicalities, we assume that the state space \mathcal{Z} is chosen such that \mathcal{E}_{\pi} is always finite. This excludes reducible processes, and we have \pi>0 on \mathcal{Z}.


The relative entropy (3.5) plays an important
role in the theory of large deviations of empirical measures. It
appears as the large-deviation rate of the empirical measure (i.e. when no time dependence is involved) of independent, identically
distributed random variables, by Sanov’s Theorem. It turns out that
the relative entropy also plays an important role in the connection
between large deviations and generalized gradient flows. In fact, we
prove below that, if detailed balance holds, then \mathcal{E}_{\pi}/2 is
exactly the right choice for the functional driving a generalized
gradient flow, in the sense that both the integrability condition and
the time symmetry condition are satisfied. We also prove the reverse
statement. With detailed balance, we can therefore connect to the
theory set out in Section 2,
and construct a generalized gradient flow with symmetric
potentials \Psi,\Psi^{*}. Note that the factor 1/2 compensates for the factor 2 in the time-symmetry relation (• ‣ ii).


We present the second main result in a compact version where the
assumptions are stronger than needed. We see the result as a principle
that holds in general contexts, but needs an extra proof for these
cases. In the next section we give possible extensions.


Theorem 3.3.

Let an empirical process
\rho^{(n)} satisfy a large-deviation principle of the form
(1.15) for all T>0 with corresponding
L-function \mathscr{L}. Assume that the invariant measure satisfies
\pi\in\mathcal{P}(\Omega)
and that \mathscr{L} is twice Fréchet differentiable near
(\rho,s)=(\pi,0). Then the time symmetry (• ‣ ii) holds
with respect to \mathcal{V}_{\mathscr{L}}=\frac{1}{2}D\mathcal{E}_{\pi} if and only if the generator \mathcal{Q} satisfies detailed balance with respect to \pi. In particular, this implies that the integrability condition (1.11) holds with \mathcal{S}=\frac{1}{2}\mathcal{E}_{\pi}.



By Theorem 2.3, it follows that \mathscr{L} generates a generalized gradient system driven by the functional \frac{1}{2}\mathcal{E}_{\pi}.


Remark 3.4. 
The twice differentiability of \mathscr{L}, which is only used for the direction
“\Rightarrow”, can be weakened by working on a suitable
subspace. This requires a subspace \mathscr{G}\subset C_{b}(\Omega) with the following properties:

1. 

\mathscr{G}_{1}:=\mathrm{span}\big(\mathscr{G}\cup\{1\}\big) is a
C_{b}-dense subset of \Dom\mathcal{Q}, and \mathcal{Q}\mathscr{G}_{1}=\{\mathcal{Q}\phi:\phi\in\mathscr{G}_{1}\} is a dense subset of L^{1}(\pi);

2. 

For every \phi\in\mathscr{G} we have \int_{\Omega}\phi\,d\pi=0 and \mathcal{Q}^{T}(\phi\pi) is a finite measure;

3. 

For every \phi,\psi\in\mathscr{G}, the function




a(\varepsilon_{1},\varepsilon_{2},\varepsilon_{3}):=\mathscr{L}\Bigl((1+\varepsilon_{1}\phi)\pi,\mathcal{Q}^{T}\bigl[(\varepsilon_{2}\phi+\varepsilon_{3}\psi)\pi\bigr]\Bigr)

(3.6)

is well-defined and twice continuously differentiable in a
neighborhood of (0,0,0).


∎


Proof.

We first prove the reverse statement.
“\Leftarrow” Since \pi\in\mathcal{P}(\Omega), detailed balance (3.4) is equivalent to (see for example [Lig85, Prop. II.5.3])




\Prob\!\left((\rho^{(n)}_{t})_{t=0}^{T}\in A\right)=\Prob\!\left((\rho^{(n)}_{t})_{t=0}^{T}\in\sigma_{T}A\right)

(3.7)

for all measurable A\subset\mathcal{D}([0,T];\mathcal{P}(\Omega)), where (\sigma_{T}\rho)_{t}:=\rho_{T-t} denotes the time-reversal. In the probabilities above the curves \rho^{(n)} are assumed to start, at t=0, from empirical measures of points drawn from \pi. Therefore, by definition of the large-deviation principle,




I_{0}(\rho_{0})+I_{T}(\rho)=I_{0}(\rho_{T})+I_{T}(\sigma_{T}\rho)


for any curve (\rho_{t})_{t=0}^{T}. Moreover, by Sanov’s Theorem I_{0}=\mathcal{E}_{\pi}, so that




\mathcal{E}_{\pi}(\rho_{0})+\int_{0}^{T}\!\mathscr{L}(\rho_{t},\dot{\rho}_{t})\,dt=\mathcal{E}_{\pi}(\rho_{T})+\int_{0}^{T}\!\mathscr{L}(\rho_{T-t},-\dot{\rho}_{T-t})\,dt.


Differentiating with respect to T then yields (• ‣ ii) with \mathcal{V}_{\mathscr{L}}=\frac{1}{2}D\mathcal{E}_{\pi}, because (\rho_{t})_{t=0}^{T} was arbitrary.


“\Rightarrow”. We now assume (• ‣ ii)
and prove the detailed-balance property (3.4)
relying only on the weakened differentiability of Remark 3.2. By the density assumption on \mathscr{G} it is sufficient to prove (3.4) for all \phi,\psi\in\mathscr{G}; fix such \phi,\psi\in\mathscr{G} and the corresponding function a defined in (3.6).


Using the definition of \mathcal{E}_{\pi}, we calculate that D^{2}\mathcal{E}_{\pi}(\pi)[s_{1},s_{2}]=\int_{\Omega}\!\frac{ds_{1}}{d\pi}\frac{ds_{2}}{d\pi}\,d\pi, and therefore




\int_{\Omega}\!\psi(\mathcal{Q}\phi)\,d\pi=\int_{\Omega}\!\phi\,d\mathcal{Q}^{T}(\psi\pi)=D^{2}\mathcal{E}_{\pi}(\pi)[\phi\pi,\mathcal{Q}^{T}(\psi\pi)].


The property of detailed balance is therefore proved if we show that for all \phi,\psi\in\mathscr{G}




D^{2}\mathcal{E}_{\pi}(\pi)[\phi\pi,\mathcal{Q}^{T}(\psi\pi)]=D^{2}\mathcal{E}_{\pi}(\pi)[\psi\pi,\mathcal{Q}^{T}(\phi\pi)].

(3.8)



To prove this, first note that since \mathscr{L}\bigl((1+\varepsilon_{1}\phi)\pi,\mathcal{Q}^{T}[(1+\varepsilon_{1}\phi)\pi]+s\bigr) is minimal at s=0, we have




D_{3}a(\varepsilon_{1},\varepsilon_{1},0)=0.


Differentiating this expression with respect to \varepsilon_{1} we find that




D_{13}a(0,0,0)+D_{23}a(0,0,0)=0.

(3.9)



Secondly, the time symmetry (• ‣ ii) with
respect to \frac{1}{2}D\mathcal{E}_{\pi} reads explicitly




\mathscr{L}(\rho,s)-\mathscr{L}(\rho,-s)=\langle D\mathcal{E}_{\pi}(\rho),s\rangle.

(3.10)

Using appropriate \rho and s we obtain




a(\varepsilon_{1},0,\varepsilon_{3})-a(\varepsilon_{1},0,-\varepsilon_{3})=2\bigl\langle D\mathcal{E}_{\pi}\bigl((1+\varepsilon_{1}\phi)\pi\bigr),\mathcal{Q}^{T}(\varepsilon_{3}\psi\pi)\bigr\rangle,


and by differentiating with respect to \varepsilon_{3} we find




D_{3}a(\varepsilon_{1},0,0)=\bigl\langle D\mathcal{E}_{\pi}\bigl((1+\varepsilon_{1}\phi)\pi\bigr),\mathcal{Q}^{T}(\psi\pi)\bigr\rangle.


Differentiating again with respect to \varepsilon_{1} yields




D_{13}a(0,0,0)=D^{2}\mathcal{E}_{\pi}(\pi)[\phi\pi,\mathcal{Q}^{T}(\psi\pi)],


which combines with (3.9) to give




D_{23}a(0,0,0)=-D^{2}\mathcal{E}_{\pi}(\pi)[\phi\pi,\mathcal{Q}^{T}(\psi\pi)].


This identity implies (3.8), since the left-hand side
is unchanged upon exchanging \phi and \psi, because
D_{23}a(0,0,0)=D_{32}a(0,0,0). This proves (3.4).


Finally, differentiating (3.10) with respect to s
provides the desired integrability condition D_{s}\mathscr{L}(\rho,0)=\tfrac{1}{2}D\mathcal{E}_{\pi}(\rho).
∎



Theorem 3.3 implies that the entropy functional (3.5) is the only functional (up to constants) for which \mathscr{L} is time-symmetric. This entropy functional enters the proof because of Sanov’s theorem, and measures the cost to deviate from the equilibrium \pi.


Remark 3.5.  Using the explicit form of \mathscr{H} from (3.1) together with Proposition 2.2(ii), we can also see more directly that detailed balance of the generator \mathcal{Q} is equivalent to the time symmetry (• ‣ ii):




\displaystyle\mathscr{H}\big(\rho,\tfrac{1}{2}D\mathcal{E}_{\pi}(\rho)+\xi\big)
\displaystyle=\int_{\Omega}\!e^{-\frac{1}{2}\log\frac{d\rho}{d\pi}-\frac{1}{2}-\xi}\big(\mathcal{Q}e^{\frac{1}{2}\log\frac{d\rho}{d\pi}+\frac{1}{2}+\xi}\big)\,d\rho




\displaystyle=\int_{\Omega}\!e^{\frac{1}{2}\log\frac{d\rho}{d\pi}-\frac{1}{2}-\xi}\big(\mathcal{Q}e^{\frac{1}{2}\log\frac{d\rho}{d\pi}+\frac{1}{2}+\xi}\big)\,d\pi




\displaystyle\!\mathop{=}^{\eqref{eq:detailed balance self-adjoint}}\int_{\Omega}\!e^{\frac{1}{2}\log\frac{d\rho}{d\pi}+\frac{1}{2}+\xi}\big(\mathcal{Q}e^{\frac{1}{2}\log\frac{d\rho}{d\pi}-\frac{1}{2}-\xi}\big)\,d\pi




\displaystyle=\int_{\Omega}\!e^{-\frac{1}{2}\log\frac{d\rho}{d\pi}-\frac{1}{2}+\xi}\big(\mathcal{Q}e^{\frac{1}{2}\log\frac{d\rho}{d\pi}+\frac{1}{2}-\xi}\big)\,d\rho=\mathscr{H}\big(\rho,\tfrac{1}{2}D\mathcal{E}_{\pi}(\rho)-\xi\big),


where we have used the linearity of \mathcal{Q} to take the constant e^{-1}
out of the parenthesis.
∎

4.1 Finite-state Markov chains


We now apply the theory of Sections 2 and 3 to continuous-time Markov chains on a finite state space \Omega=\{1,\ldots,J\}. In this case we can identify




\displaystyle\mathcal{Z}:=\mathcal{P}(\{1,\ldots,J\})=\bigg\{\rho\in\mathbb{R}^{J}_{+}:\sum_{j=1}^{J}\rho_{j}=1\bigg\},


and the generator \mathcal{Q}:\mathbb{R}^{J}\to\mathbb{R}^{J} can be identified with a Markov intensity matrix Q\in\mathbb{R}^{J\times J}, i.e.




\displaystyle Q_{ij}\geq 0\qquad\text{for }i\neq j,

and

\displaystyle\sum_{j=1}^{J}Q_{ij}=0.

(4.1)

The natural tangent and cotangent spaces to \mathcal{P}(\{1,\ldots,J\}) are




\displaystyle T_{\rho}\mathcal{Z}=T^{*}_{\rho}\mathcal{Z}:=\bigg\{s\in\mathbb{R}^{J}:\sum_{i=1}^{J}s_{i}=0\bigg\},


with the usual Euclidean inner product \langle s,\xi\rangle:=s\cdot\xi.


Particle system and large deviations.


We now take independent Markov processes X_{1}(t),X_{2}(t),\ldots in \{1,\ldots,J\} with generator matrix Q. By identifying probability measures on \{1,\ldots,J\} with vectors in \mathbb{R}^{J}, the empirical process (1.13) is replaced by




t\mapsto\rho^{(n)}_{t}:=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{k=1}^{n}\mathds{1}_{X_{k}(t)},


which is a random variable in \mathcal{P}(\{1,\ldots,J\}) that counts the weighted number of particles at each site. Under suitable initial conditions, this process converges almost surely to the solution of (1.16). We prove in Theorem A.1 in the Appendix that a corresponding large-deviation principle (1.15) holds in BV\!\big(0,T;\mathcal{P}(\{1,\ldots,J\})\big) with the weak-* topology, with




\displaystyle\mathscr{L}(\rho,s)=\sup_{\xi\in T_{\rho}^{*}\mathcal{Z}}\xi\cdot s-\mathscr{H}(\rho,\xi),

and

\displaystyle\mathscr{H}(\rho,\xi)=\sum_{i,j=1}^{J}\rho_{i}Q_{ij}\left(e^{\xi_{j}-\xi_{i}}-1\right)\!.

(4.2)




Towards generalized gradient flows.


Let \pi\in\mathcal{P}(\Omega) be invariant, i.e. Q^{T}\pi=0. We implicitly assume that \pi has only non-zero coordinates If \pi_{i}=0 for some i, then the space \mathcal{Z} needs to be restricted to those \rho for which \rho_{i}=0.. The relative entropy functional (3.5) then becomes




\mathcal{E}_{\pi}(\rho)=\sum_{i=1}^{J}\rho_{i}\log\frac{\rho_{i}}{\pi_{i}}.


For this application, the role of the detailed-balance condition will appear explicitly in the calculations; let us not assume this condition for now. Following the construction from Lemma 2.3, we define (taking \mathcal{S}=\tfrac{1}{2}\mathcal{E}_{\pi})




\displaystyle\Psi_{\mathscr{L}}^{*}(\rho,\xi)
\displaystyle:=\mathscr{H}\big(\rho,\tfrac{1}{2}D\mathcal{E}_{\pi}(\rho)+\xi\big)-\mathscr{H}\big(\rho,\tfrac{1}{2}D\mathcal{E}_{\pi}(\rho)\big)




\displaystyle=\sum_{i,j=1}^{J}\rho_{i}Q_{ij}\left[\exp\!\left(\frac{1}{2}\log\frac{\rho_{j}}{\pi_{j}}+\xi_{j}-\frac{1}{2}\log\frac{\rho_{i}}{\pi_{i}}-\xi_{i}\right)-\exp\!\left(\frac{1}{2}\log\frac{\rho_{j}}{\pi_{j}}-\frac{1}{2}\log\frac{\rho_{i}}{\pi_{i}}\right)\right]




\displaystyle=\sum_{i,j=1}^{J}\sqrt{\rho_{i}\rho_{j}\frac{\pi_{i}}{\pi_{j}}}Q_{ij}\left(e^{\xi_{j}-\xi_{i}}-1\right)\!.

(4.3)

Under a condition of weak reversibility (cf. [Mie11b]),




Q_{ij}>0\iff Q_{ji}>0\qquad\text{for all }i,j=1,\ldots J,

(4.4)

expression (4.3) can be written as:




\displaystyle\Psi_{\mathscr{L}}^{*}(\rho,\xi)
\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i,j=1}^{J}\left[\sqrt{\rho_{i}\rho_{j}\frac{\pi_{i}}{\pi_{j}}}Q_{ij}\left(e^{\xi_{j}-\xi_{i}}-1\right)+\sqrt{\rho_{i}\rho_{j}\frac{\pi_{j}}{\pi_{i}}}Q_{ji}\left(e^{\xi_{i}-\xi_{j}}-1\right)\right]\!




\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i,j=1}^{J}\sqrt{\rho_{i}\rho_{j}Q_{ij}Q_{ji}}\bigg(\cosh\!\Big(\xi_{j}-\xi_{i}+\frac{1}{2}\underbrace{\log\frac{Q_{ij}\pi_{i}}{Q_{ji}\pi_{j}}}_{=0\text{ if d.b. holds}}\Big)-1\bigg).

(4.5)

From this form it is immediate that \inf_{\xi}\Psi_{\mathscr{L}}^{*}(z,\xi)=0=\Psi_{\mathscr{L}}^{*}(z,0) whenever the detailed balance condition (3.4) holds. By (1.9a) and (1.9b), this implies that \Psi,\Psi^{*}\geq 0. Therefore, under the condition of detailed balance, the linear system (1.16) is described by the symmetric generalized gradient system (\mathcal{P}(\{1,\ldots,J\}),\Psi_{\mathscr{L}},\tfrac{1}{2}\mathcal{E}_{\pi}), as prescribed by Theorem 3.3.


Remark 4.1. 
In general, the explicit formula for \Psi_{\mathscr{L}} can become much more involved than the formula for \Psi_{\mathscr{L}}^{*}. For example, \Psi_{\mathscr{L}}^{*} is linear in Q, while \Psi_{\mathscr{L}} is not.
∎


To illustrate the principle of generating a generalized gradient structure out of the large deviations, we describe two examples; one for which detailed balance holds, and one for which it does not.


Example 4.2 (finite-state Markov chain with detailed balance).

For this example we take J=2; then detailed balance (3.4) always holds whenever (4.4) holds. We now write s=(s_{1},-s_{1}) and \xi=(\xi_{1},-\xi_{1}). Then (4.5) can be written as




\Psi_{\mathscr{L}}^{*}(\rho,\xi)=\sqrt{\rho_{1}\rho_{2}Q_{12}Q_{21}}\big(\cosh(2\xi_{1})-1\big),


and its dual becomes




\Psi_{\mathscr{L}}(\rho,s)=\sqrt{\rho_{1}\rho_{2}Q_{12}Q_{21}}\bigg(\cosh^{*}\!\Big(\frac{s_{1}}{2\sqrt{\rho_{1}\rho_{2}Q_{12}Q_{21}}}\Big)+1\bigg),


where \cosh^{*} is the Legendre transform of the hyperbolic cosine. By Theorems 2.3 and 3.3, we know that the entropy functional \mathcal{S}_{\mathscr{L}} has to be the relative entropy (3.5), and we find




\mathscr{L}(\rho,s)=\Psi_{\mathscr{L}}(\rho,s)+\Psi^{*}_{\mathscr{L}}\big(\rho,-\tfrac{1}{2}D\mathcal{E}_{\pi}(\rho)\big)+\tfrac{1}{2}D\mathcal{E}_{\pi}(\rho)\cdot s,


where the left-hand side is the large-deviation function, and the right-hand side describes a generalized gradient system. Note especially that \Psi_{\mathscr{L}} and \Psi_{\mathscr{L}}^{*} are indeed symmetric, but not quadratic in s and \xi.



Example 4.3 (finite-state Markov chain without detailed balance).

We now take J=3 and




Q:=\begin{pmatrix}-1&1&0\\
0&-1&1\\
1&0&-1\end{pmatrix}\!.


The invariant measure is \pi=(1/3,1/3,1/3), but detailed balance does not hold. Therefore, we can no longer apply Theorem 3.3, so that we can not tell a priori whether the integrability condition (1.11) holds.


Therefore, we need to go one step back to Proposition 2.2.
We have the explicit formula
\mathscr{H}(\rho,\xi)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\eqref{eq:Markov Lagrangian}}}{{=}}\rho_{1}e^{\xi_{2}-\xi_{1}}+\rho_{2}e^{\xi_{3}-\xi_{2}}+\rho_{3}e^{\xi_{1}-\xi_{3}}-1 and find




\displaystyle\mathcal{V}_{\mathscr{L}}(\rho)
\displaystyle:=D_{s}\mathscr{L}(\rho,0)=\argmin\mathscr{H}(\rho,\cdot)=\frac{1}{3}\begin{pmatrix}\log\big(\rho_{1}/\rho_{3}\big)\\
\log\big(\rho_{2}/\rho_{1}\big)\\
\log\big(\rho_{3}/\rho_{2}\big)\end{pmatrix}\!.


By Proposition 2.2(i), we can still use this covector field \mathcal{V}_{\mathscr{L}} to construct \Psi_{\mathscr{L}},\Psi_{\mathscr{L}}^{*} such that:




\mathscr{L}(\rho,s)=\Psi_{\mathscr{L}}(\rho,s)+\Psi^{*}_{\mathscr{L}}\big(\rho,-\mathcal{V}_{\mathscr{L}}(\rho)\big)+\mathcal{V}_{\mathscr{L}}(\rho)\cdot s.


The right-hand side of this equation however, does not represent a generalized gradient system, since the vector field \mathcal{V}_{\mathscr{L}}(\rho) is non-conservative, i.e. the integrability condition (1.11) breaks down.
